results.title: BIRTH ORDER AND THE INTRAHOUSEHOLD ...
results.content: If all parents were forced to have the same number of children, the model predicts that the educational attainment of these children would be the same, on average, and hence there would be no birth order effect. Human capital outcomes will, of course, vary within the household because the children have different endowments, but because the amount of resources given to each child is the same and genetic endowments are independent of birth order, we will not see any birth order effects. In summary, the model shows that a birth order effect in intrahousehold allocation can arise even without assump-tions about parental preferences for speciﬁc-birth-order children or genetic endowments varying by birth order. We show, using a model of intrahousehold allocation with endogenous fertil-ity, that birth order effects can arise even without parents having stronger preferences for children with speciﬁc birth order or the endowments of the children being related to birth order.

results.title: Intrahousehold Resource Allocation and Child Food Poverty in the United States | Review of Economics of the Household | Springer Nature Link
results.content:
Title: Intrahousehold Resource Allocation and Child Food Poverty in the United States | Review of Economics of the Household | Springer Nature Link
Utilizing the U.S. Consumer Expenditure Survey (CES) within a collective household framework, this study empirically estimates intrahousehold resource allocation in the U.S., with a specific emphasis on the resource shares allocated to children. Children’s resources in collective households: Identification, estimation, and an application to child poverty in Malawi. Utilizing a collective household framework and data from the U.S. Consumer Expenditure Survey (CES), we show that the number of children in a household has a lesser impact on the combined share of resources allocated to parents, but significantly influences the share of resources for the children. In this section, we employ a structural approach to estimate whether the allocation of resources to each household member diminishes as the number of children increases.Footnote 1 Furthermore, we investigate the extent to which it propels each household member towards a situation of food poverty. To achieve the goal of identifying each household member’s resource share through household consumption data, the DLP model assumes the resource share is independent of household expenditure, such that the identification can be accomplished by comparing the Engel curves of private goods without the observable price variations (Please refer to the Appendix: Identification Assumptions for further details). We select clothing as the private assignable good for estimating household members’ resource shares, a commonly suggested private assignable good (Browning et al., 1994. Figure 1 presents the estimated resource shares for men, women, and children across household income levels for the full sample. Estimated resource shares for men, women, and children across household income levels. Estimated resource shares for men, women, and children across household income levels and household sizes. In this study, we propose a method that combines the estimated allocation of household resources with USDA food plans, aiming to deliver a reliable and standardized approach to assessing individual food poverty. Table 5 presents individual-level food poverty rates for each household type by comparing each household member’s allocated resource with the corresponding minimum food budget, revealing which household members are more likely to experience food poverty. By using the estimated resource shares and the USDA Thrifty Food Plan, we introduce an objective method for assessing the risk of food poverty for each household member.
